How Much Do Creators Actually Make?

How much do creators actually make? The honest answer: it depends on platform, audience country, niche, and how many income streams are stacked. This post gives planning ranges from public 2026 creator reports, then shows why multi-stream income beats any single platform.

By platform, per 1,000 views (2026)

Platform / formatPer 1,000 views
YouTube long-form (by niche)$1–$17
YouTube Shorts$0.02–$0.15
TikTok Creator Rewards$0.04–$1.00
Instagram Reels$0.03–$0.30
Twitch ads (CPM share)$0.70–$2.00 effective

By monthly income tier (multi-stream, gross)

TierTypical setupMonthly grossTake-home (US, est.)
Hobby10k subs, ad-only$200–$800~85–90%
Part-time50k subs + sponsors$2,000–$6,000~70–78%
Full-time200k subs, 4 streams$10,000–$30,000~60–70%
Top 1%1M+ subs, media company$50,000+varies (S-corp)

Take-home estimates use a simplified self-employment model; real tax depends on deductions and entity.

The multi-stream rule of thumb

Ad revenue alone rarely supports a full-time income. The stack that does: ads (base) + sponsorships (3–10× ads) + memberships/subs (predictable) + affiliate/Shop (scales with trust). A mature full-time creator typically earns 3–5× ad-only income this way. Model your own stack with the YouTube Money Calculator.

Frequently asked questions

What do most YouTubers earn?

Most channels under 100k subs earn less than $2,000/month gross — and after taxes and reinvestment, far less. The median YouTuber earns well below a median US salary; only the top few percent clear six figures.

Do Twitch streamers make more than YouTubers?

Per engaged audience hour, often yes (subs + Bits are generous), but the audience ceiling is lower. Most serious creators are on both, plus a short-form platform.
